Adult Puget Sound rockfish typically reach a maximum total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], a modest size relative to many other members of the genus Sebastes. This ultimate length is attained after several years of steady somatic growth in the cold, productive waters of the northeastern Pacific. In contrast, the length at which individuals first achieve reproductive maturity is considerably smaller, with puberty occurring at a total length of 12.2 centimeters [Lp = 12.2 centimeters]. This developmental milestone marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the transition to a reproductively active adult life history. Field surveys conducted in the Puget Sound basin indicate that males and females both reach this size threshold during their second or third year of life, though local variation in food availability may slightly alter the timing. The relatively small size at puberty is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy in which early reproductive investment is favored despite the constraints imposed by a cool thermal environment.

The maximum reproductive output of Puget Sound rockfish has been quantified under controlled experimental conditions. Gravid females held at a stable water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C] produced approximately 156 offspring per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 156 offspring per spawning event], and available data indicate that a single reproductive bout occurs each year [F_R_i = single reproductive bout occurs each year], yielding a maximum annual reproduction rate of approximately 156 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 156 offspring per year]. This annual reproductive frequency is typical of temperate viviparous rockfishes, where the energetic demands of gestation limit the number of broods per annum. The combined daily reproduction rate derived from these figures is thus a product of the fecundity per event and the event frequency, reflecting the species' modest but sustained reproductive effort. Comparisons with congeners of similar body plan suggest that this level of output is consistent with an income-breeding strategy, wherein females fuel reproduction largely from concurrent foraging rather than stored reserves.

The extremely small mass of individual larvae at parturition highlights the high degree of maternal investment in offspring number over offspring size. Newly released larvae have an estimated neonatal wet weight of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value derived from the approximate 0.8-millimeter egg diameter and the assumption of a spherical egg shape, though the viviparous mode of development introduces some uncertainty. This minute initial size places the species among the smallest-born rockfishes in the northeast Pacific. In contrast, the asymptotic body mass achieved by adults is substantially greater. The ultimate wet weight for fully grown individuals is 75.6 grams [Wwi = 75.6 grams], a value consistent with the length-weight relationship established for this population. This marked disparity between neonatal and adult mass underscores the rapid relative growth trajectory that characterizes the juvenile phase.

Sexual maturation is also accompanied by a distinct size-specific body mass, and the time to this developmental milestone has been characterized. Individuals at the onset of puberty weigh approximately 22.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 22.7 grams], a value that aligns closely with the weight predicted from the length-weight relationship at the documented length at puberty, and this mass is typically attained approximately two to three years after birth [tp = approximately two to three years after birth]. This mass threshold represents a critical juncture at which energy allocation shifts from purely somatic growth to include gonadal development. The attainment of 22.7 grams typically occurs during the same growing season in which the fish reaches 12.2 centimeters in total length, suggesting a tight coupling between length and mass in this species. Compared to other Sebastes species inhabiting similar latitudes, the mass at puberty for Puget Sound rockfish is relatively low, a pattern that may reflect the selective pressures of a short growing season and the need to begin reproduction before the onset of winter resource limitation.

Lifespan data for Puget Sound rockfish indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This extended lifespan is noteworthy given the species' modest maximum body size and early age at maturity, a combination that places it toward the slower end of the life-history continuum among small-bodied rockfishes. The thermal regime of the Puget Sound basin, characterized by cool, stable temperatures near 11 °C, is thought to contribute to this extended longevity by reducing metabolic rates and slowing the accumulation of oxidative damage over time. Comparisons with captive-reared individuals show that those held at slightly elevated temperatures exhibit reduced maximum ages, supporting the view that temperature exerts a strong influence on the rate of senescence. The combination of a 22-year lifespan, small body size, and moderate annual reproductive output defines a relatively stable, low-turnover population dynamic that is vulnerable to overexploitation.
